design_detail: Prospective cohort within the Netherlands XTC Toxicity (NeXT) study. 188 ecstasy-naive volunteers aged 18 to 35 who intended to start using ecstasy were tested between April 2002 and April 2004, then sent drug-use questionnaires every 3 months for about 18 months. Within 3 years, people who had started using ecstasy and persistently ecstasy-naive people individually matched on sex, age and verbal IQ were retested with the same battery by an examiner blind to ecstasy use. Analysed: 58 people who started using ecstasy and 60 who did not; 12 test scores covering attention, working memory, verbal and visual memory and visuospatial ability.
can_establish: Whether, among young adults who intended to try ecstasy and had the same test scores beforehand, those who went on to use small amounts changed differently on memory and other tests over about one to one and a half years from those who did not.
cannot_establish: That ecstasy caused the smaller verbal-memory gains (not randomized; the groups differed in cannabis and cocaine use, in retest interval and, in the wider cohort, in sensation seeking); that the change reflects neurotoxicity (no brain measure in this paper); whether it lasts, grows with heavier use or reverses after stopping (one retest after very little use); or that it matters in daily life (all scores stayed in the normal range).

sample.recruitment: Volunteers aged 18 to 35 who were considering starting ecstasy use soon, recruited April 2002 to April 2004 by targeted site sampling (dance events, youth fairs, universities, colleges, parks), a project website and internet campaign, and snowball sampling; main inclusion criterion an intention to probably or certainly use ecstasy for the first time in the near future, preferably with one or more friends who already did. Paid 100 or 150 euros per session (Methods › Participants, p. 729).
sample.inclusion_exclusion: Excluded: earlier ecstasy use, a major medical, neurological or neuropsychiatric disorder or cognition-affecting medication in the last year, pregnancy, intravenous drug use. Required abstinence from psychoactive substances for at least 2 weeks and from alcohol for at least 1 week before each examination, checked by urinalysis (p. 729).
sample.demographics: Ecstasy group at baseline: 25 men and 33 women, age 21.8 (SD 3.1), DART-IQ 103.4 (9.0); comparison group: 25 men and 35 women, 21.5 (2.1), 105.5 (10.2). Most had senior general secondary education or vocational college (45 of 58 vs 55 of 60) (Table 1, p. 731). Similar on sex (chi-square 0.03, p = .88), age (t = -0.67, p = .50), verbal IQ (t = 1.18, p = .24) and education (U = 1563, p = .13) (p. 731).
sample.attrition: Of 188, 158 returned the last drug-use questionnaire (30 refused or could not be reached); 64 of the 158 reported starting ecstasy and 59 of them attended the follow-up session; 61 matched controls were chosen from the 94 who stayed naive (p. 730). One person who had started using ecstasy was excluded for a cocaine-positive urine test and one control for dyslexia and attention-deficit disorder diagnosed in youth (p. 731). Dropouts and the 5 people who started using ecstasy but did not attend are not compared with those analysed.
sample.selection_effects: Volunteers selected for an intention to use ecstasy, more educated and intelligent than young adults in general and, by the authors' account, highly motivated (p. 734). The comparison group consists of people who did not start despite intending to, chosen by matching only after those who had started using ecstasy were known, so they were retested later. In the wider cohort, starting ecstasy went with higher sensation seeking (p. 733).

exposure.measurement: Self-report on validated substance-use questionnaires sent every 3 months and at follow-up: cumulative number of tablets and weeks between first and last use (Methods › Independent Variables, p. 730). Urinalysis before sessions for recent use. No hair testing; tablet content not tested (the authors cite Dutch pill testing showing that 95% of tablets sold as ecstasy in 2003 and 2004 contained MDMA as the major component, p. 734).
exposure.dose_frequency_duration_route: At follow-up, cumulative 3.2 (SD 5.2) tablets, median 1.5, range 0.5 to 30; time since first tablet 18.6 (17.6) weeks; time since last tablet 11.8 (12.0) weeks, median 7.9, range 2 to 59; duration of use printed as 6.8 (12.5) weeks, median 0.0, range 0 to 12 (Table 1, p. 731; see reporting issues). The text describes use over a mean of 1.6 months within an average follow-up of 11.1 months (p. 731). Route not reported.
exposure.polysubstance: Alcohol, tobacco, cannabis, amphetamine and cocaine use in the last year measured at both sessions and entered as log-transformed covariates (pp. 730-731). Cannabis was higher in the ecstasy group at baseline (mean 48.8 vs 17.2 joints in the last year, medians 15.8 vs 15.5; U = 1363, p = .04) and at follow-up (53.6 vs 20.5 joints, U = 1089, p < .001), and cocaine at follow-up (1.4 vs 0.3 times, U = 1436, p = .006); amphetamine at follow-up 2.9 (SD 20.5, range 0 to 156) times vs none (Table 1, p. 731). A sensitivity analysis excluded everyone who had used cocaine or amphetamines, leaving 43 and 57 (p. 732).
exposure.abstinence_at_testing: At least 2 weeks from psychoactive substances and 1 week from alcohol before each session, checked by urinalysis (p. 729); last ecstasy use 11.8 (12.0) weeks before follow-up, minimum 2 weeks (Table 1, p. 731).

comparison.controls: 60 persistently ecstasy-naive members of the same at-risk cohort, individually matched on sex, age and verbal IQ measured with the Dutch Adult Reading Test (p. 729).
comparison.matching: Matched on sex, age and DART-IQ (p. 729); similar on education (p. 731). The abstract also describes the groups as matched on use of substances other than ecstasy (p. 728), which Table 1 contradicts for cannabis and cocaine.
comparison.unmeasured_premorbid: Cognition was measured before use in both groups and did not differ. Sensation seeking, impulsivity and depression were measured in the wider cohort but are not covariates here (p. 733); sleep, lifestyle and the settings of use were not measured.
comparison.controls_other_drug_use: Yes, at lower levels: cannabis (mean 17.2 joints in the last year at baseline), alcohol, tobacco and a little cocaine (0.3 times); no amphetamine (Table 1, p. 731).

outcomes.instruments: Paced Auditory Serial Addition Test at 2.4 s and 1.6 s; Dutch adaptation of Digit Span forward and backward; Rey Auditory Verbal Learning Test (sum of 5 learning trials of 15 words, delayed recall and recognition after 20 minutes); computerized Memory for Designs (elements over 5 trials, number of trials, delayed reproduction), split into two parallel versions; Mental Rotation Task; adapted Judgment of Line Orientation (pp. 729-730).
outcomes.validity_norms: Performance of all participants remained within the normal range of a sex- and age-comparable general population (p. 732). Parallel versions are described for Memory for Designs only (p. 730); whether a different word list was used for the retest of the RAVLT is not stated.
outcomes.operationalization: Change from baseline to follow-up, analysed with ecstasy use and sex as fixed factors and age, DART-IQ, log-transformed use of other substances and the baseline score as covariates; RAVLT recognition, near ceiling, was dichotomized into any decline vs none and analysed by logistic regression (p. 730).
outcomes.multiplicity_correction: None; p < .05 for every test, and the dose-response correlations were one-tailed (pp. 730, 732). Editors' calculation: with a Bonferroni threshold for 12 outcomes (p < .0042), none of the three significant group results (p = .02 to .03) would remain.
outcomes.assessor_blinding: The examiner was blind to whether a participant had used ecstasy (p. 729).

analysis.effect_sizes: Change scores, ecstasy group (58) vs comparison group (60), with adjusted regression coefficients (Table 2, p. 732): RAVLT immediate recall +0.86 (SD 5.5) vs +3.90 (5.8) words, B 2.23 (95% CI 0.17 to 4.29), F(1, 108) = 4.62, p = .03, partial eta squared 0.04; delayed recall -0.52 (1.8) vs +0.65 (1.8) words, B 0.63 (0.05 to 1.22), F(1, 108) = 4.67, p = .03, partial eta squared 0.04; recognition: any decline in 22.4% vs 6.7%, odds ratio 5.87 (Wald chi-square 5.62, p = .02; the table prints 1.77 (1.36 to 25.37), see reporting issues). No differences on Memory for Designs, Digit Span, PASAT, Judgment of Line Orientation or Mental Rotation (p = .21 to .85). Baseline: no differences on any test (multivariate F(12, 96) = 0.73, p = .72, partial eta squared 0.08) (p. 731). Sensitivity analysis without anyone who had used cocaine or amphetamines (43 vs 57): delayed recall effect F(1, 92) = 6.62, p = .01, partial eta squared 0.07 (p. 732). Dose-response within the ecstasy group (one-tailed): cumulative tablets with delayed recall change r = -0.24, p = .04, and recognition change r = -0.29, p = .02, not immediate recall (r = -0.16, p = .12); partial correlations controlling for age, IQ, sex and other substances, recognition r = -0.30, p = .02, delayed recall r = -0.21, p = .08; logistic regression for recognition decline, log-transformed tablets odds ratio 15.18 (95% CI 1.10 to 210.14), raw tablets 1.30 (0.96 to 1.75), p = .09; no association with duration of use or time since last use (p. 732). Editors' calculation from Table 2: unadjusted standardized differences in change about 0.54 (immediate recall) and 0.65 (delayed recall); adjusted coefficients divided by the change-score SD about 0.39 and 0.35; recognition decline in 13 of 58 vs 4 of 60 people (crude odds ratio 4.0, risk difference 16 percentage points); two-tailed p for the dose correlations about .07 (delayed recall) and .03 (recognition).
analysis.covariates: Sex (fixed factor), age, DART-IQ, log-transformed use of alcohol, tobacco, cannabis, amphetamines and cocaine, and the baseline score (p. 730). Not adjusted for the difference in retest interval or for sensation seeking.
analysis.preregistration_detail: The paper refers to a separate design article for the NeXT study (ref. 48, not read); no registration of hypotheses or outcomes is reported.
analysis.selective_reporting: All 12 outcomes are reported in Table 2. The sensitivity analysis excluding people who had used cocaine or amphetamines is reported for delayed recall only, not for immediate recall or recognition (p. 732). Recognition was analysed as a dichotomy in the group comparison but as a continuous change score in the dose correlations (pp. 730, 732).
analysis.power: Not reported. The confidence intervals of the significant adjusted differences reach close to zero (0.17 words for immediate recall, 0.05 for delayed recall) and the recognition odds ratio interval runs from 1.36 to 25.37.

interpretation_gap.results_show: With no differences before use, people who started using ecstasy (median 1.5 tablets) gained less than the comparison group on word-list learning and delayed recall at retest, and more of them lost any points on recognition (13 vs 4 people, on a test where almost everyone scores about 30 of 30); 9 other scores did not differ; all scores stayed in the normal range; the ecstasy group was retested about 8 months sooner and used more cannabis and cocaine.
interpretation_gap.claimed: The abstract concludes that even a first low cumulative dose of ecstasy is associated with decline in verbal memory (p. 728), and the conclusion calls the finding "suggestive for Ecstasy-induced neurotoxicity" (p. 734). For immediate recall the ecstasy group did not decline (58.7 to 59.6 words); it gained less than the comparison group, whose gain the authors call a normal retest effect (p. 732). No brain measure is reported in this paper. The abstract says the groups were matched on use of substances other than ecstasy, while the Methods matched on sex, age and verbal IQ only and Table 1 shows more cannabis and cocaine in the ecstasy group. Against this, the authors state that the design offers no indisputable evidence of causality, that the immediate clinical relevance is limited and that the study cannot say whether the effects remain after quitting (pp. 728, 733-734).

timeline.event: This study: the first prospective cohort of people tested before their first ecstasy use.

Murphy et al. name it the only genuinely prospective study among 33 studies of executive and visuospatial memory, with no visuospatial (line orientation) difference, and describe mean use as 3.2 tablets after 3 years (pp. 166, 172-173).
Halpern et al. note that the median of 1.5 tablets at follow-up raises doubt about a causal role of ecstasy (Discussion, 4th paragraph).
Ung et al. cite it among studies reporting neurocognitive impairment in people with light use (p. 282).

replication.where_it_stands: No replication with the same design is described in the papers read in this batch; whether one exists has not been checked. Murphy et al. (2009) note that prospective studies in this field take years and risk too little use by follow-up, and that experimental exposure would be unethical (pp. 172-173). The finding remains a single small-effect result after very little use.

funding.funder: Netherlands Organization for Health Research and Development (ZonMw), grant 310-00-036, Addiction Program (p. 734).
funding.affiliations_note: Amsterdam Institute for Addiction Research; Academic Medical Center, University of Amsterdam; University Medical Centre Utrecht; Bonger Institute of Criminology. Recorded as a flag for closer reading only.

what_would_settle_it: A larger prospective cohort with longer follow-up and a wide range of later use, retesting the comparison group at the same intervals with parallel test forms, hair-verified exposure, adjustment for cannabis, cocaine and sensation seeking, one pre-registered primary memory outcome, and further retests after people stop.

domains.note: Baseline cognition equal and the baseline score adjusted for; other substances measured at both sessions and adjusted for; but cannabis and cocaine use rose more in the ecstasy group, and sensation seeking, sleep and lifestyle were not adjusted for.
Self-reported tablets of unknown content, very little variation (median 1.5); the duration row of Table 1 is internally inconsistent.
At-risk volunteers; 16% lost before follow-up and 5 of the 64 people who started using ecstasy not retested; controls chosen by matching from 94 after those who had started using ecstasy were known.
No intervention after exposure is described.
Those lost to follow-up and the people who started using ecstasy but did not attend are not compared with those analysed.
Blind examiner and standardized tests, but the retest interval differed by 8 months between groups, a parallel RAVLT form is not reported, and recognition was at ceiling and dichotomized.
12 outcomes without correction; sensitivity analysis shown for one outcome; one-tailed dose tests.

risk_of_bias.reasoning: This is the strongest design among the papers read: cognition was measured before any ecstasy use, the groups were matched and equal at baseline, and the examiner was blind. The overall judgment is high because several concerns act together on a small effect whose intervals reach almost to zero: differential retest intervals, residual confounding by cannabis and cocaine, possible practice effects on a repeated word list, and 12 uncorrected outcomes. The study may be cited for smaller verbal-memory retest gains after very little ecstasy use in this cohort. It may not be cited as showing that ecstasy damages memory or serotonin neurons, or that the change is lasting or clinically meaningful.

key_findings.finding: Before any ecstasy use, the 58 people who later started and the 60 who did not showed no significant difference overall on the 12 test scores in one multivariate analysis of covariance (F(12, 96) = 0.73, p = .72, partial eta squared 0.08); the 12 scores were not tested one by one at baseline.
The Methods state that the same participants also underwent brain imaging, analysed and described by other investigators in separate articles, within the same project.
key_findings.note: This is the paper's own evidence that the imaging cohort published as de Win et al. (2008) is this same 188-person sample, which a narrative review in this batch presents as a second prospective cohort (card sc_parrott_2013, reporting issues).

key_findings.finding: RAVLT immediate recall (sum of 5 trials) changed by +0.86 (SD 5.5) words in the ecstasy group vs +3.90 (5.8) in the comparison group (58.7 to 59.6 vs 57.8 to 61.7); adjusted B 2.23 (95% CI 0.17 to 4.29), F(1, 108) = 4.62, p = .03.
key_findings.locator: Results › Neuropsychological Testing, 2nd paragraph (p. 731); Table 2, RAVLT immediate row (p. 732)

key_findings.finding: RAVLT delayed recall changed by -0.52 (SD 1.8) words vs +0.65 (1.8) (13.8 to 13.2 vs 13.5 to 14.1, of 15); adjusted B 0.63 (95% CI 0.05 to 1.22), F(1, 108) = 4.67, p = .03.
key_findings.locator: Results › Neuropsychological Testing, 2nd paragraph (p. 731); Table 2, RAVLT delayed recall row (p. 732)

key_findings.finding: RAVLT recognition (of 30, mean scores 29.95 to 29.66 vs 29.88 to 29.93): any decline in 22.4% vs 6.7% of people; logistic regression odds ratio 5.87 (Wald chi-square 5.62, p = .02).
key_findings.locator: Table 2, RAVLT recognition row and footnote (p. 732); Results › Neuropsychological Testing, 2nd paragraph (begins p. 731, continues p. 732)
key_findings.note: Editors' calculation: 13 of 58 vs 4 of 60 people; crude odds ratio 4.0.

key_findings.finding: No group differences in change on Memory for Designs (immediate, trials, delayed), Digit Span forward and backward, PASAT at 2.4 s and 1.6 s, Judgment of Line Orientation or Mental Rotation (p = .21 to .85); no sex x ecstasy interaction on RAVLT scores.
key_findings.locator: Table 2 (p. 732); Results › Neuropsychological Testing, 2nd paragraph (begins p. 731, continues p. 732)

key_findings.finding: After excluding everyone who had used cocaine or amphetamines (43 people who had started using ecstasy, 57 controls), the delayed recall effect remained significant (F(1, 92) = 6.62, p = .01, partial eta squared 0.07); cocaine and amphetamine use had a covariance effect on delayed recall, alcohol, tobacco and cannabis did not.
key_findings.note: Editors' arithmetic: 15 of the 58 people in the ecstasy group and 3 of the 60 controls were excluded as having used cocaine or amphetamines.

key_findings.finding: Within the ecstasy group, cumulative tablets correlated with change in delayed recall (r = -0.24, p = .04) and recognition (r = -0.29, p = .02) but not immediate recall (r = -0.16, p = .12), all one-tailed; after adjustment only recognition remained (partial r = -0.30, p = .02; delayed recall -0.21, p = .08); recognition decline with log-transformed tablets odds ratio 15.18 (95% CI 1.10 to 210.14), with raw tablets 1.30 (0.96 to 1.75), p = .09; no association with duration of use or time since last use.
key_findings.locator: Results › Relationship Between Neuropsychological Test Performance and Amount of Ecstasy Use, 1st and 2nd paragraphs
key_findings.note: Editors' calculation: two-tailed p about .07 for delayed recall and .03 for recognition. The odds ratio of 15.18 for recognition decline with log-transformed tablets has an interval from 1.10 to 210.14, spanning more than two orders of magnitude; it must never be quoted without that interval and cannot carry a dose-response claim.

key_findings.finding: Use at follow-up: 3.2 (SD 5.2) tablets in total, median 1.5, range 0.5 to 30, over a mean of 1.6 months; last use 11.8 (12.0) weeks before retest (median 7.9). Time between sessions 11.1 (6.2) months in the ecstasy group vs 19.1 (7.5) in the comparison group (t = 6.30, p < .001).
key_findings.locator: Table 1; Results › Characteristics of the Sample and Substance Use, 2nd and 3rd paragraphs

key_findings.finding: Other substances: cannabis higher in the ecstasy group at baseline (48.8 vs 17.2 joints in the last year, p = .04) and at follow-up (53.6 vs 20.5, p < .001), cocaine higher at follow-up (1.4 vs 0.3 times, p = .006); smoking, alcohol, amphetamines and cocaine similar at baseline.
key_findings.locator: Table 1; Results › Characteristics of the Sample and Substance Use, 2nd and 3rd paragraphs

key_findings.finding: Overall test performance of all participants remained within the normal range of a sex- and age-comparable general population.

The authors list alternatives to an ecstasy effect: cannabis, cocaine and amphetamine use, sensation seeking (higher in people who started using ecstasy in the wider cohort), depression and expectancy from the information given at entry; and limitations: no indisputable evidence of causality, self-reported medical history, unmeasured lifestyle and settings, longer follow-up for controls (argued not to explain the result because retest effects shrink with time), uncontrolled tablet content and a well-educated, motivated sample; and, in the other direction, that a well-educated sample makes a decrease in cognitive function harder to detect (the brain-reserve argument), so that the study may have underestimated an effect of ecstasy.
key_findings.locator: Comment, 2nd paragraph (begins p. 732) and 6th paragraph (begins p. 733)

reporting_issues.issue: Table 1 gives duration of ecstasy use as 6.8 (SD 12.5) weeks with median 0.0 and range 0 to 12. With 58 values between 0 and 12 and at least half at 0, the mean can be at most 6.0 and the SD at most about 6 (editors' arithmetic). The text's mean period of 1.6 months fits a mean of about 6.8 weeks, so the printed range is probably wrong.
reporting_issues.consequence: The spread of duration of use cannot be read from the table.

reporting_issues.issue: Table 2 prints the recognition result as B 1.77 (95% CI 1.36 to 25.37). 1.77 is the logarithm of the odds ratio of 5.87 given in the text and the table footnote, while the interval is the interval of the odds ratio itself (its logarithms, 0.31 and 3.23, centre on 1.77; editors' calculation).
reporting_issues.consequence: Read as printed, the estimate and its interval are on different scales; the odds ratio is 5.87 (95% CI 1.36 to 25.37).

reporting_issues.issue: Memory for Designs rows in Table 2 do not fit their own means: for number of trials the comparison group's mean fell from 3.4 to 3.1 but its change score is printed as +0.10; for delayed reproduction its mean rose from 20.8 to 20.9 but its change is printed as -0.33, with change SDs of 1.8 although the score SDs are 0.5 and 0.3 (an SD of a difference cannot exceed 0.8 here; editors' arithmetic).
reporting_issues.consequence: Errors in non-significant rows; they do not affect the verbal-memory results but lower confidence in the table.

reporting_issues.issue: The abstract states that the groups were matched on use of substances other than ecstasy (p. 728); the Methods matched on sex, age and verbal IQ (p. 729), and Table 1 shows more cannabis (baseline and follow-up) and cocaine (follow-up) in the ecstasy group (p. 731).
reporting_issues.consequence: The abstract overstates the comparability of the groups; other drug use was adjusted for statistically, not matched.

reporting_issues.issue: The title and abstract describe the ecstasy group as having minimal exposure to other drugs, but 15 of 58 had used cocaine or amphetamines (editors' arithmetic from the sensitivity analysis), one person reported 156 amphetamine uses, and cannabis use was higher than in the comparison group.
reporting_issues.consequence: Minimal is relative to earlier studies; the sensitivity analysis without people who had used cocaine or amphetamines covers delayed recall only.

reporting_issues.issue: The conclusion that low doses are associated with decreased verbal memory function is described as decline, but immediate recall did not fall in the ecstasy group (58.7 to 59.6 words); the difference is a smaller practice gain than in the comparison group.
reporting_issues.consequence: Decline is accurate for delayed recall and recognition only; for immediate recall the finding is a smaller improvement.

verification.source_read: PDF, pp. 728-736 (all pages; Tables 1 and 2 checked on rendered pages; p. 736 also carries an unrelated correction notice; no supplementary material)

disagreements.first_pass: Before any ecstasy use, the 58 people who later started and the 60 who did not showed no differences on any of the 12 test scores (multivariate F(12, 96) = 0.73, p = .72, partial eta squared 0.08).
disagreements.reviewer: AI reader 31, note on key finding 0: confirmed, but this is a single multivariate test, not 12 separate ones, and any claim built on it should say so.
disagreements.resolution: Checked at p. 731 (Results, Neuropsychological Testing, 1st paragraph) and the Methods (p. 730): the baseline comparison is one MANCOVA with ecstasy use and sex as fixed factors. Corrected: no differences on any of 12 scores claimed more than the paper reports. The same correction is proposed for cl_mdma_prospective.

disagreements.reviewer: Missed (AI reader 31): Methods, p. 729, state that the same participants underwent brain imaging described by other investigators in separate articles, which settles whether de Win et al. (2008) is a second cohort.
disagreements.resolution: Checked at p. 729: the sentence is there, in the study-design paragraph. Added as a key finding because two claims and one narrative review turn on whether that imaging cohort is the same sample.

disagreements.first_pass: Editors' calculation: two-tailed p about .07 for delayed recall and .03 for recognition.
disagreements.reviewer: Missed (AI reader 31): the card reports the odds ratio of 15.18 (1.10 to 210.14) but does not say that an interval spanning two orders of magnitude cannot carry a dose-response claim.
disagreements.resolution: Checked at p. 732: the interval is as printed. Added to the note, because the figure is the study's only quantitative dose-response result and is easy to quote on its own.

disagreements.first_pass: The authors list alternatives to an ecstasy effect: cannabis, cocaine and amphetamine use, sensation seeking (higher in people who started using ecstasy in the wider cohort), depression and expectancy from the information given at entry; and limitations: no indisputable evidence of causality, self-reported medical history, unmeasured lifestyle and settings, longer follow-up for controls (argued not to explain the result because retest effects shrink with time), uncontrolled tablet content and a well-educated, motivated sample.
disagreements.reviewer: Missed (AI reader 31): p. 734, the authors argue from the brain-reserve hypothesis that their well-educated sample may have led them to underestimate the effect, a limitation that runs against their own result's direction.
disagreements.resolution: Checked at p. 734: the argument is there, in the limitations paragraph. Added to the same key finding, so that the list of limitations is not one-sided.
